items.title: L4: Reading a sample advert closely
items.source: Civil Service Jobs adverts; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Imagine an advert for an Administrative Officer in a department's regional office. It gives a salary range, a permanent contract and a working pattern of full time, with part-time and job-share options considered. The summary says the team processes claims and answers enquiries from the public. The responsibilities list checking forms, updating records, answering calls and emails, and passing complex cases to an Executive Officer. The essential criteria say the applicant must have the right to work in the UK, be able to communicate clearly in writing and speech, and be able to work accurately with data. A desirable criterion is experience of using spreadsheets. The advert says that applications are assessed in two ways: a sift based on the behaviours Communicating and Influencing and Delivering at Pace, followed by an online test and an interview for those who pass. It states that the security check is the Baseline Personnel Security Standard and that the post is open to UK nationals and certain other nationalities. It says that the closing date is on a stated date and time, that interviews will take place on stated dates by video, and that a named contact can answer questions and arrange adjustments. When you read an advert like this, work through it in order. Mark each essential criterion and ask whether you can give an example for it. Note the behaviours, because they are what you will write about. Note the dates and put them in your diary at once.

items.title: L4: Deciding whether to apply
items.source: Civil Service Jobs adverts; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Applying takes time, so it helps to decide quickly whether a vacancy suits you. Start with the essentials. Check eligibility, including nationality and right to work. Check the location and working pattern to see whether you can attend the office on the days required. Check the closing date. Then read the essential criteria. If you can meet them all, you are a candidate. If you miss one that is truly essential, such as a required professional qualification, the sift will normally reject you, and your time is better spent on another vacancy. If the criterion is worded as ability or experience, think about whether you have it from unpaid or home life as well as paid work. Running a household budget, helping run a club or caring for a relative can all show organisation, accuracy and communication. Next look at the desirable criteria. You do not need them all. Then check the assessment methods. If the process includes timed tests and you struggle with them, consider asking for an adjustment or choose to practise first. Finally consider fit: the salary, the commute, the security level and the hours. A job that you cannot afford to travel to or cannot do at the hours required will not work, however good the application. If you are unsure about a detail, contact the department before you decide. Be honest with yourself about both strengths and gaps.

items.title: L4: Turning everyday experience into evidence
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Many people think they have no experience that counts, but the Civil Service accepts evidence from paid and unpaid life. Running a household budget shows accuracy, planning and handling money. Caring for children or relatives shows organisation, patience and dealing with many demands at once. Volunteering at a food bank, a school or a community group shows teamwork, reliability and communication. Helping a neighbour fill in forms shows plain English and attention to detail. Studying or training, even informally, shows you can learn. A good example answers the question that was asked, uses I to show what you personally did, and gives a result. A weak example is vague, describes only the situation, or claims a team's work as your own. Compare two statements. Weak: We organised a fundraising event and it went well. Stronger: I organised a coffee morning for 40 people. I made a list of tasks, asked six volunteers to bring cakes, arranged the room, took the money and counted it. We raised 310 pounds for the school, and the head asked me to do it again. The stronger statement gives numbers, actions and a result. Use real names of roles but do not give private details about other people. Be ready to be asked follow-up questions at interview about anything you write. Never make up an example. Assessors are used to people who have not had a conventional career and will judge what you show, not where you got it.

items.title: L4: Handling online tests in practice
items.source: Civil Service Jobs; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Online tests reward both skill and good habits. Before the test, read the invitation for the time allowed, the number of questions and any rules about calculators. If it says a calculator is allowed, have one ready. Practise with sample questions in the same format. Aim to do some each day in the week before. Check your device, browser and internet connection, and charge the device. Choose a quiet place, tell the people you live with that you need a clear slot, and put your phone on silent. On test day, read the instructions in full even if you think you know them. Work out how long you have for each question. If a question takes too long, make your best guess, mark it if the test allows, and move on. Do not leave questions blank unless told there is a penalty, because most tests do not take marks off for a wrong answer. In a verbal reasoning test, use only the text. In a numerical test, write down the figures you need and check units such as pounds or thousands. In a situational judgement test, choose the response that follows the Civil Service Code and the behaviours: honest, fair, safe, calm and willing to ask for help. If your connection drops, contact the number or email in the invitation straight away and describe what happened. Do not try to start the test again unless you are told to.

items.title: L4: Video interviews: logistics and conduct
items.source: Civil Service Jobs; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Many Civil Service interviews are held by video. The invitation gives the date, time, platform and the names or number of panel members. Confirm that you can attend as soon as you receive it. Look at the instructions for joining, and test your camera, microphone and connection a day or two before. Choose a quiet room with plain background and good light facing you. Keep your phone silent. Have your ID ready if asked. Have a glass of water and a notepad or notes if notes are allowed. Check that your name on screen is your real name. Join a few minutes early. Dress as you would for an office interview. Look at the camera when you speak, which feels like eye contact, and speak slightly more slowly than usual because of delays. If the connection fails, stay calm, try to rejoin and contact the number in the invitation. The panel will usually be two or three people. One will lead and others will write notes. They will ask all candidates the same questions. Use STAR for behaviour questions. Pause and think before you answer. If you need the question repeated, ask. At the end, you may be asked if you have questions. Have one prepared about the team or the work. Say thank you. Afterwards, write down what went well and what you would change. This helps whether you are successful or not.

items.title: L4: Stages and timings in practice
items.source: Civil Service Jobs; Civil Service Recruitment Principles
items.body: The stages of a Civil Service recruitment follow a pattern, but the timing varies. Adverts often stay open for one to a few weeks. After the closing date, the sift usually takes some days or weeks, depending on how many applications arrive. If tests are used, you are normally given a window of days to complete them. Interviews are held on dates set in the advert, and departments often try to give notice of a few days to a couple of weeks. After interviews, results can take days or weeks. Pre-employment checks can then take several weeks, longer if references are slow or security clearance is needed. The whole process from closing date to start date commonly takes some weeks to a few months. Do not treat any of these as fixed, because they depend on the department and campaign. What matters is that you plan with flexibility and keep checking your email. If you are waiting, you can contact the department to ask where things stand, politely and no more than needed. Keep applying to other roles in the meantime. It is common to have more than one application at different stages. If you receive a second conditional offer, tell the department you prefer to decline politely rather than leaving it unanswered. Do not resign from your current job until you have a confirmed written start date, because a conditional offer can still be withdrawn if the checks are not cleared.

items.title: L4: Pre-employment checks: handling real situations
items.source: Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Pre-employment checks can feel stressful, but most are routine if you prepare. Identity: you will be asked for original documents. A passport is the usual choice. If you do not have one, other documents such as a driving licence plus proof of address may be accepted, depending on the department's list. Check the list in the offer email and gather documents early. If something is missing or out of date, contact the department straight away. Right to work: UK nationals show a passport or a birth certificate with an official document showing National Insurance number. People with immigration status may use an online share code. Employment history: you give details of the last three years or so. If you were at home looking after children, in education, unemployed or unwell, say so and give a contact or document that can confirm it. References come from employers or other people who know you. Choose people who will reply quickly, tell them to expect the request, and give accurate contact details. Criminal record: declare unspent convictions honestly. Rules on spent convictions exist so that old offences do not always count against you. Not declaring something is a bigger problem than the conviction. If your name has changed, bring the document that shows the change, such as a marriage certificate. If you are struggling to collect something, explain to the department and ask what alternatives are possible.

items.title: L4: After the offer: notice, resigning and the first day
items.source: Civil Service Jobs; GOV.UK, Your rights and notice periods
items.body: A conditional offer is not yet a job. Once the checks are cleared you receive a confirmed start date, often with a contract or a statement of terms. Check the details: job title, grade, salary, location, working pattern, hours and start date. If something differs from the advert, ask. Only after that should you give notice to your current employer. Look at your own contract to see your notice period. Many jobs require one or more weeks, and some require a month or more. Your new start date should allow for it. If your notice period is longer than the department can wait, talk to the department early, because they may agree a later start or ask whether you can negotiate a shorter notice with your employer. Be polite when you resign, in writing, and keep a copy. Leave on good terms, because you may need a reference. Before your start, the department may send details of the induction, such as the time, place, what to bring and who to ask for. Bring the identity documents they list. On the first day you meet your line manager, collect equipment and a pass, and learn about security, data protection and the Civil Service Code. Nobody expects you to know everything. Ask questions. Keep notes. If you are working from home, check that your equipment and any security arrangements are ready before you start.

items.title: L4: Fair recruitment: spotting what is and is not unfair
items.source: Civil Service Commission, Recruitment Principles; Equality Act 2010
items.body: Fair recruitment means that candidates are assessed against the same criteria, by the same methods, on merit, and without discrimination. It is helpful to know what fairness looks like in practice. It is fair for an advert to set essential criteria that relate to the job, such as the right to work or the ability to use a computer. It is fair for a department to give a test to all candidates and to use the same pass mark. It is fair to turn down someone who does not meet the criteria. It is fair for a panel to ask follow-up questions about an example. It is fair to give a disabled candidate extra time in a test as a reasonable adjustment, because this removes a disadvantage rather than giving an advantage. It is not fair to reject someone because of their age, sex, race, religion, disability or another protected characteristic. It is not fair for a panel member to give extra marks to a friend, or to ask different candidates different questions without a reason. It is not fair to hide information from some candidates that others can see. If you think a recruitment was unfair, first raise it with the department using its complaints process. You can ask for feedback to understand the decision. If you remain unhappy, you can bring a complaint about a breach of the Recruitment Principles to the Civil Service Commission. Keep a record of dates, names and what was said.

items.title: L4: Disability Confident and adjustments: applying it
items.source: Disability Confident scheme, GOV.UK; Equality Act 2010
items.body: Disability Confident and reasonable adjustments work together but are different things. The guaranteed interview offers an interview to a disabled applicant who meets the minimum criteria. Reasonable adjustments are changes that help someone take part in the process or the job. A person can use either or both. To use the interview commitment, say on the application that you are disabled and want to be considered under it. The panel should not see the details of your condition. Your answers are scored in the same way as everyone else's. A person with dyslexia might ask for extra time in a test and for documents in a different colour or font. A person who is deaf or hard of hearing might ask for a British Sign Language interpreter or for questions in writing. A person with a mobility impairment might ask for an interview room with step-free access. A person with anxiety might ask for a break between stages or the interview questions in advance. A person with a long-term health condition might ask for flexible working or a quiet place. Describe the effect on you and what would help. You do not need to give your full medical history. If the first adjustment does not work, ask for another. The department decides what is reasonable, but it must consider your request properly and not refuse because of a general view about cost.

items.title: L4: Flexible working in practice
items.source: GOV.UK, Flexible working; Civil Service Jobs adverts
items.body: Flexible working covers several arrangements. Part time means fewer hours than full time, for example four days a week, or school hours. Job share means two people share one full-time job. Compressed hours mean working your full hours in fewer days, such as nine days a fortnight. Flexitime means you choose start and finish times within core hours. Hybrid means some days at the office and some at home. Term-time working means working during school terms only. The Civil Service advertises many roles as open to flexible working, and the advert will say if it is not possible, for example if a role needs someone on a public counter at set times. Employees have a statutory right to request flexible working, and employers must handle the request in a reasonable manner. From the first day of employment you can make a request. If you want a particular pattern, ask when you are offered the job or before. Be specific about the days and hours and explain how work will be covered. For example: I would like to work Monday to Thursday, nine to four. I am happy to be contactable on Friday for urgent matters. Think about the effect on your pay, pension and leave, which are normally reduced in proportion to the hours. Agreed patterns are written into your contract or a statement of terms. You can also ask later, after you have settled in.

items.title: L4: Using feedback and reserve lists to improve
items.source: Civil Service Jobs; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Feedback is one of the most valuable things you can get from a recruitment. Not all departments give detailed feedback, but many do if you ask politely, usually using the contact in the outcome email. Feedback may be a score, a short comment against each criterion or a note on how close you were to the pass mark. Read it calmly and look for patterns. If it says your examples lacked detail, work on using numbers and actions. If it says you did not answer the question, practise reading questions carefully and underlining the key words. If it says you did not provide enough evidence of a behaviour, prepare more examples for that behaviour. Keep a notebook of examples and feedback so that your answers improve. A reserve list is different. If you reached the standard but there was no post, you may be put on a list and offered a later vacancy, often within a set period such as 12 months, if the advert says so. Being on the list means your application is still live, so keep your contact details up to date. If a vacancy is offered, reply promptly. If you are not on the list, do not be discouraged. Another campaign will have a different mark and different competition. Practise with a friend, read the advert, and apply again. Persistence and learning from each attempt are the most common route to success.
